title: Composers who lost credit: Rosetta and Until the Real Thing Comes Along
summary: Goodwin says Henri Woode wrote Rosetta, which Earl Hines got credit for, and a dancer named Van wrote the song Andy Kirk made famous.

bands.name: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I would like to ask a rather provocative question that Mr. Taylor wrote here. Did one man sometimes get credit for another's ideas? What do you think about that, Crook? Can you give us any examples of that?
Definitely. Some years back -- back in the early '30s there was a number composed, "Rosetta". Henri Woode, There was a composer by the name of Henry Woods, which at that time was unknown.
Was he a Kansas City musician?
He was around Kansas City. I can't say that Kansas City was his home. I don't think so.
Piano. He was a wonderful arranger and composer. He wrote a number called "Rosetta" and he wrote another called "Jeannette", which didn't ever make the big time.
Are you speaking of the "Rosetta" that we all feel that Earl Hines wrote?

Right. That's Henri Woodle's number. I was playing with him when he composed that. I was the first person that did the vocals on it, and several numbers he has written that -- well, they didn't hit the big time but he was a good writer, and somehow or another Earl Hines -- I don't know whether he bought the number or whether he just out right took it but he got the credit for "Rosetta" because his band featured it with Walter Fuller doing the vocals and -- but that was Henri Woodle's number.
There was another little dancer here in town that wrote a number that Andy Kirk made famous, "Until the Real Thing Comes Along".
Oh, that was a big hit.

That was a big hit; that was composed by a little fellow by the name of Van. He was a dancer and he played around on piano and he composed -- he got that together and he had some different words and the tune had a different name.
He composed it as the "Slave Song". When Andy

recorded it, it was "Until the Real Thing Comes Along". Phia Terrell, Fay Terrell, one of my very best friends, did a beautiful job on the vocals, and those are some of the numbers that the composers didn't get credit for.
